extracted.intended_audience: aspiring stand-up comedians, comedy writers, and performers
extracted.subtask_description: Glossary-style how-to guidance for writing, rehearsing, and performing stand-up comedy routines, covering joke structure, timing, stagecraft, crowd work, and professional practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: hurry a joke / rush a joke
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicating a joke to an audience faster than they can comprehend the Setup's relationship to the Punchline, which can diminish or kill the laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To 'hurry a joke' means to deliver the punchline too quickly, without allowing the setup to build properly; example: missing the perfect pause before the punchline leads to weaker audience reaction. See also 'processing'.

rubrics_metrics.name: hurt line
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjective psychological tipping point when the pain within the comedy becomes real and turns mood into drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'hurt line' is a sharp, cutting remark intended to sting or embarrass; it can leave the room stunned before laughter. Use with caution: crossing the hurt line risks turning comedy into drama (example: violent or cruel actions that feel real). See 'dramedy'.

rubrics_metrics.name: joke structure (setup, punchline, connector, target assumption, reinterpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke is often two sections: Setup and Punchline, linked by the 5 mechanisms (Greg Dean): 1st Story, Target Assumption, Connector, Reinterpretation, 2nd Story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Setup establishes a Target Assumption (expected meaning of the Connector); Punchline provides a Reinterpretation (unexpected interpretation) that shatters the Target Assumption. Use the Connector (one thing with two interpretations) to create surprise. See 'joke diagram', 'joke structure by Greg Dean', and 'reveal'.

rubrics_metrics.name: reveal
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific information, words, phrases, or actions that communicate the Reinterpretation, which is best placed near or at the end of the Punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put the reveal close to the punchline ending to maximize surprise. Poor placement or signaling can weaken the joke's effect. See 'Reinterpretation' and 'step on a laugh'.

rubrics_metrics.name: telegraphing
rubrics_metrics.description: Causing the audience to guess the Punchline before it's delivered, usually because the Setup has too much information or an acting choice that leads the audience prematurely to the idea of the punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telegraphing is an anti-pattern; avoid giving too much information in the setup or signaling the punchline with acting choices. See 'misdirection' and 'joke structure'. (Submitted by Scotty Meltzer.)

rubrics_metrics.name: pause / take a beat
rubrics_metrics.description: Stopping talking after a punchline to allow time for the audience to laugh or silence during a performance to enhance tension or allow thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pause after punchlines to let laughter peak; 'take a beat' is often used between Setup and Punchline or after Punchline. Proper pausing helps avoid 'step on laughs' and allows momentum for the next joke. See 'one-liner timing' and 'stay in the bit'.

rubrics_metrics.name: one-liner timing
rubrics_metrics.description: After delivering a punchline, wait for the laugh to peak, then pause for a count (2, 3, 4), then start the next setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One-liner timing is a specific pause practice to preserve laughs; relates to tag timing. Proper timing prevents killing or stepping on laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: tag / tag timing
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional short punchline immediately following a punchline that does not require a new setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tags to extend laughs; time tags so they don't interrupt the laugh peak. Tag timing contributes to 'roll' (continuous laughter). See 'tag line' (British).

rubrics_metrics.name: step on laughs / talk over laughs
rubrics_metrics.description: After delivering a Punchline, when comedians continue talking (instead of pausing), causing the audience to stop laughing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid speaking over laughter; common mistakes ('step on laughs') will 'kill a laugh' and reduce momentum. See 'kill a laugh', 'pause', 'talk over laughs', and 'reveal'.

rubrics_metrics.name: stay in the bit
rubrics_metrics.description: After a Punchline during audience laughter, stop talking and remain in the same emotion or state of mind as when the joke was delivered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staying in the bit gives the audience permission and space to laugh and keeps momentum for the next joke. Coined by Jerry Seinfeld. See 'pause' and 'timing'.

rubrics_metrics.name: timing (comedy timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The tempo and rhythm developed between the comedian and the audience while performing; also estimating length of routines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing includes pauses, beats, tag timing, and pacing of setups and punchlines. Good timing is central to effective delivery and depends on reading the audience (feedback loop). See 'comedy timing' and 'relationship with the audience'.

rubrics_metrics.name: laughs per minute (LPMs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measurement for counting the number of laughs in routines or shows (e.g., goal: 5 laughs per minute).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LPMs are a quantitative metric for routine success and progression toward professional standards. Abbreviation: LPMs. See 'laughs per minute' and 'routines'.

rubrics_metrics.name: kill / kill a laugh / killed
rubrics_metrics.description: To 'kill' means to have a performance where the audience continuously laughs; 'kill a laugh' refers to speaking or acting after a joke that causes laughter to stop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Want to 'kill' a show (consistent laughs). Avoid 'killing a laugh' by not stepping on laughs or ruining timing. 'Killed' often used to describe strong shows. See 'scream' and 'roll'.

rubrics_metrics.name: roll
rubrics_metrics.description: Delivering a string of jokes and tags that cause the audience to continuously laugh for an extended period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achieve a 'roll' with well-placed tags, timing, and momentum. Connects to LPMs and tag timing. Example: 'I crushed it because I got the audience on a roll.'

rubrics_metrics.name: read on material
rubrics_metrics.description: When comedians perform their jokes and judge the audience's responses (laughter, groans, boos, silence, applause) to know how to adjust their script to get consistent laughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use audience feedback to rewrite, drop, or tailor material; essential part of development and road work. See 'feedback loop' and 'tailor'.

rubrics_metrics.name: tailor material
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpreting or altering material to fit a unique performing situation and different audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust jokes for audience demographics or context (example: cops in audience). Tailoring helps material land; see 'deregulate' and 'Rehearsal Process'.

rubrics_metrics.name: mic technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Most effective ways of holding and moving the microphone, stand, and cord to enhance communication and smoothly get performers on and off stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good mic technique affects clarity and stage presence; includes microphone choices (cardioid, omnidirectional, wireless) and handling. See 'microphone', 'mic', and 'mic stand'.

rubrics_metrics.name: smooth on and smooth off (entrance/exit best practices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Best practices for getting on stage and off stage to ensure well-run shows (phrase coined by Jerry Seinfeld).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smooth stage transitions preserve show pacing and professionalism; helps maintain audience momentum. See 'entrance' and 'exit'.

rubrics_metrics.name: respect the light / red light / run the light
rubrics_metrics.description: Signals to comedians about their allotted performing time; 'the light' warns when a set is almost over; 'red light' is the final signal to end immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complying with the light preserves relationships with clubs; running the light can get you banned. 'Run the light' is unprofessional. See 'light' and 'get the light'.

rubrics_metrics.name: set / set list / show list
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'set' is a comedian's routine(s) for a show; a set list/show list is a bullet-point reminder of the order of jokes or routines to be done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use set lists to organize material and pacing. Repeating sets across performances involves consistent delivery, timing, and material interpretation. See 'Rehearsal Process'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearsal Process
rubrics_metrics.description: Greg Dean's method of turning jokes or routines into scenes by acting them out using Narrator, Self, and Character POVs so comedians remember in pictures, sounds, and feelings rather than rote words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acting scenes during rehearsal helps performers 'tell the story' rather than recite lines, improving recall and performance. See related warnings about 'improper rehearsal' and 'self talk'.

rubrics_metrics.name: improper rehearsal / self talk
rubrics_metrics.description: Practicing jokes by repeating words aloud over and over (coding them in Broca's area) which can make recall dependent on internal verbal cues ('self talk').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid improper rehearsal; instead rehearse scenes and images so recall is rooted in feeling and picture, not just words. See 'Rehearsal Process' and 'talking head'.

rubrics_metrics.name: storytelling / storytelling joke structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Telling vivid narratives that evoke emotions; in stand-up, storytelling uses Narrator POV, scene work, POV shifts, and may distribute Setup, Punchline, and Tag across Narrator, Self, and Character POVs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Storytelling requires acting, staging, tenses, psychology, and scene work; more complex than one-liners. Use POV shifts effectively. See 'Anatomy of Funny Storytelling' and 'scene work'.

rubrics_metrics.name: scene work / POVs (Narrator, Self, Character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting up scenes and acting them out from different POVs to portray roles and create the humor of situations, characters, and conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scene work builds storytelling jokes and requires practicing Self and Character POVs for believable performances. See 3 POVs and 'Rehearsal Process'.

rubrics_metrics.name: rule of three / rhythm of three
rubrics_metrics.description: Joke format where a Setup lists two positive items, then the Punchline reveals a third negative/unexpected item (variant name: rhythm of three).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the rule/rhythm of three as a reliable joke template; examples provided. See 'joke formats' and 'rule of three'.

rubrics_metrics.name: punch up / punch down
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Punch up' refers to making jokes about higher-status targets; 'punch down' makes jokes about lower-status targets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punching up is generally recommended ethically and artistically; punching down risks cruelty and crossing the 'hurt line'. Also 'punch up' can mean adding tags and jokes to material.

rubrics_metrics.name: crowd work / riff
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques of interacting with the audience (crowd work) and taking an audience member's response and embellishing it to discover humor (riff).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Riffing is a core improv/crowd-work skill; keep it responsive and use it to generate new material. See 'improv' and 'ad-lib'.

rubrics_metrics.name: inside joke
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor based on common-knowledge information only known by a select institution, group, or people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inside jokes can reward small groups but exclude general audiences; be aware of audience composition to avoid unintelligible jokes. Example: 'only two people got it.' See 'common knowledge'.

rubrics_metrics.name: public domain (topics and premises)
rubrics_metrics.description: Topics and premises are not owned by anyone; while individual jokes have a natural copyright, they're difficult to enforce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat topics/premises as common material; be cautious when accusing plagiarism because legal enforcement is rare and requires proof of financial harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: mic / microphone choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Microphone types and characteristics (cardioid, omnidirectional, wireless) and their effect on performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and handle microphones to suit the room and style; mic choice affects volume, proximity, and movement. See 'mic technique' and 'PA system'.
